sections.text: An adapter takes an iterator and gives you a new iterator that changes the items in some way. You chain adapters with dots, like a pipeline. The most common ones are map (change each item), filter (keep only some items), enumerate (add a counter), zip (pair two iterators), take and skip (limit the number of items), chain (join two iterators) and rev (go backwards).

Adapters are lazy. Calling map doesn't run your closure, it only builds a new iterator that will run it later, when someone asks for items. Here nothing happens until the for loop pulls the values out:

Look at the Output comment. The first line comes before any doubling, and then "doubling" and "got" alternate: each loop turn asks for one item, and only then does the closure run. Rust even warns you if you build an adapter and never use it.

A for loop is not the only way to use up an iterator. collect() gathers the items into a collection. The type annotation, here Vec<i32>, tells collect what to build. The next lesson covers collect and other ways to finish. Now a pipeline of three adapters:

(1..=10) is a range of the numbers 1 to 10 (including 10), and ranges are iterators. filter calls its closure with a reference to each item (a &i32 here), and keeps the item when the closure returns true. n % 2 works on the reference as well, but when you compare the value itself you need to write *n, for example *n > 5. map receives the item itself and returns a new one.
The other adapters, one by one:
enumerate and zip give you tuples, which a for loop can take apart right in the pattern, as in for (i, name). zip stops as soon as the shorter iterator runs out.
Think of an assembly line. Each adapter is a station that looks at an item, changes it or throws it away, and passes it on. Nothing moves until someone at the end asks for the product.

This is like Java Streams, C# LINQ, JavaScript array methods and Python generators, with one big difference: Rust's whole chain of adapters is compiled into a single loop with no intermediate lists, so it is usually as fast as a hand-written loop. Unlike JS array methods, nothing runs until you consume the iterator, and filter's closure borrows the item (&Item).

exercise.prompt: The starter prints every word. Change the loop so it goes through an iterator pipeline instead: keep only the words longer than 3 letters, and turn each one into uppercase before it is printed. It should print three lines: APPLE, BANANA and KIWI. Hint: words.iter().filter(|w| w.len() > 3).map(|w| w.to_uppercase())

quiz.question: What happens when you write let d = v.iter().map(|x| x * 2); and never use d?
options: Every item is doubled right away and the results are stored inside d
The program panics, because d is never used
Nothing: map is lazy, so the closure never runs unless something consumes d

quiz.question: What does zip do?
options: Joins two iterators end to end into one longer iterator
Pairs up the items of two iterators as tuples
Removes the items that appear in both iterators

quiz.question: What does enumerate give for each item?
options: A tuple of (index, item), counting from 0
Only the index, as a usize, and the item is dropped
A tuple of (item, item) from two neighbouring positions
